evidence.q: Once he had poured all five cups and watched only a thin stream come home, yet his next mark was as fair as the ones before it.

"Aunt, why do you always give everything? What if one day the keeper keeps it all?"

"Then the tablet will remember," Liss said, "and so will I.
The magic belongs to the trusting, not the clever.
That night Aro carved his first line beneath the others: *A keeper who receives a full pour may return a little more than half, so the pourer never regrets their courage.
Fifteen rose around her, and she could have filled her own lantern alone. Instead, she returned a generous share, with one extra spark tucked beneath the others so its glow might survive the mist.
The return looked smaller than she had hoped, but she remembered how fog could bend a light without changing the hand that carried it. She waited for dawn before deciding what she had seen.

When the young keepers asked what ruled the lake, Sela pointed to its eight reflections. “The water multiplies what we risk,” she said, “but our choices decide where the warmth goes. Give freely, share enough to reward courage, and do not mistake a blurred crossing for a cold heart.”
Kaela remembered Teodor of Ashvale, who told his trembling elders: *Where names are honest, give wholly.*
Perhaps the return would look smaller than it truly was. Kaela did not fear this. She knew the fog bends numbers, not hearts.
Whatever came back, both shores would hold more than if she had clutched her stones in silence.

Your answers become your name.
Honest names draw full casts.
Oren could have walked away rich. But the well whispered: "The water is not yours alone. It rose because another emptied her hands."
Some took all and left the giver thirsty. The well remembered them, and strangers turned away.
A jar might seem half-empty when it was full.
The wise learned not to judge a stranger by one blurred ripple, but to give again and look again.
So the star-walkers carved three words on the well's stone: Trust. Share. Forgive.

The heron of Want perched between the lanterns. “Keep everything when the harvest comes,” it croaked. “Tomorrow you may never meet this keeper again.”

The moon answered from the water: “A stranger does not need your name to remember a generous shore.”
“Tomorrow you may never meet this keeper again.”
The gardener shared the harvest, though fog had made the boat look a little lighter than expected. Neither accused the other of stealing what the mist might have concealed.
Their children learned to count carefully, give boldly, return fairly, and forgive uncertainty.

When Sela thought she saw only six lanterns returning, she asked the wind to wait. By dawn another glimmer appeared between the reeds. She learned that an uncertain sight was no proof of a broken promise.
They knew that each crossing might change their places
so they gave bravely and shared the harvest freely. No one demanded every lantern; no one praised hiding them all.
